info.bio: Red Hot Chili Peppers es un grupo de California fundado en 1983 que combina funk y rock. Es otro de los grupos de rock que despuntaron en los 90, atravesaron varias barreras musicales y fueron muy originales, creando su propio estilo de música de rock explosivo. Red Hot Chili Peppers se formó en el contexto de una cultura underground nacida a principios de los 80 en California, que se caracterizaba por la recuperación de los grandes clásicos del funky y por una incipiente cultura del hip hop.

scenes.name: George Clinton en los ochenta: Atomic Dog
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: Con Casablanca hundida y Bogart muerto (1982), Warner censurando la portada de The Electric Spanking of War Babies y la radio negra vetándolo, Clinton vendió a Capitol cientos de horas grabadas. «Atomic Dog» (Computer Games, 1982), segundo single casi olvidado, fue número 1 R&B cuatro semanas sin entrar en el Top 100 pop: quizá el gancho más sampleado de todos los tiempos, himno de los Omega Psi Phi, copiado por Karyn White, Teddy Riley o Ice Cube. Colaboraciones malditas (Sly, James Brown en 1980, Thomas Dolby, Vanessa Williams, Prince en Paisley Park), el segundo disco de los Red Hot Chili Peppers (1985), Letterman y Lollapalooza. Desde 1988, con «Bring the Noise» de Public Enemy sobre «Get Off Your Ass and Jam», el loop de P-Funk superó a James Brown como sample preferido (Schooly D, EPMD, De La Soul) y Digital Underground se declaró «Sons of the P». El ritmo del One se filtró hasta en la música más mecánica, el hip hop.

scenes.name: Funk rock: Chili Peppers, Primus y la Black Rock Coalition
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: A los blancos les era mucho más fácil tocar funk y grabar: Jane’s Addiction debutó con un directo, Primus de Les Claypool (devoto de Larry Graham), los Limbomaniacs con Bootsy y Maceo, Praxis. Los Red Hot Chili Peppers de Anthony Kiedis y Flea, con Freaky Styley producido por Clinton (1985), versionaron a Sly, los Meters y Stevie y llevaron a P-Funk al escenario de los Grammy de 1993; pero los creadores del funk rock, como los P-Funk All Stars, no tenían esa libertad. En Nueva York Living Colour de Vernon Reid no conseguía contrato pese a tener a Mick Jagger de fan, y Reid y Greg Tate fundaron en 1985 la Black Rock Coalition: «El rock and roll es música negra y nosotros somos sus herederos», contra el «rock de orientación apartheid». Abrió paso a Steve Coleman, Me’Shell NdegéOcello, James Blood Ulmer o el Kelvynator de Kelvyn Bell.

scenes.name: Gang of Four
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: Estudiantes del departamento de Bellas Artes de la Universidad de Leeds (T. J. Clark, ex situacionista; Terry Atkinson, de Art and Language) que llevan Brecht, Godard y Gramsci al rock: un meta-rock autocrítico. De la admiración por Dr. Feelgood pasan al punk funk con el bajo de Dave Allen: guitarra astillada de Andy Gill con amplificadores a transistores («Gang of Four estaba en contra del calor»), anti-solos, nada de zapadas, todo a pie de igualdad como en el funk de James Brown. Damaged Goods (Fast Product, 1978) desmenuza el amor con el lenguaje del comercio; con EMI se niegan a cambiar «rubbers» en Top of the Pops y Entertainment! (1979), seco y sin reverb, es una de las obras maestras del postpunk. Solid Gold (1981) rockea más. Su gran legado florece en Estados Unidos: Red Hot Chili Peppers, Minutemen, Fugazi, Big Black, Rage Against the Machine, The Rapture.

scenes.name: Funk-metal
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Una de las grandes ideas de fusión de los ochenta: integrar los ritmos y voces brutales del funk y el rap con el metal de guitarras. Los Red Hot Chili Peppers descubren lo que tenían en común George Clinton y Jello Biafra; Fishbone y su fusión satírica de funk, ska y soul; Faith No More, híbrido inventivo de punk, funk, progresivo, hip hop y metal (Introduce Yourself, Angel Dust); Victim's Family.

podcast.title: Early Formation of the Classic Lineup (1988-1989)
podcast.body: Following the death of Hillel Slovak and the departure of Jack Irons in June 1988, the band auditioned Dwayne "Blackbird" McKnight, but he didn't work out. John Frusciante joined as guitarist in October 1988, followed by Chad Smith as drummer in December 1988. By early 1989, this new lineup of Frusciante, Smith, Flea, and Anthony Kiedis formed what would become known as the classic Red Hot Chili Peppers configuration, debuting on the album "Mother's Milk." "By the start of 1989, the Chili Peppers had undergone a complete refurbishment. John was the new guitarist and Chad was the new drummer."

podcast.title: "Blood Sugar Sex Magik" Recording Location (April 1991)
podcast.body: For the recording of "Blood Sugar Sex Magik," the Red Hot Chili Peppers moved into a historic mansion at 351 Laurel Canyon Boulevard, built in 1918. The house, with a reputation for being haunted and allegedly having secret tunnels to the nearby "Houdini Estate," was chosen by producer Rick Rubin for its isolated vibe. A Canadian company converted the basement into a recording studio. Chad Smith, however, was too unnerved by the house's atmosphere to stay there during sessions. "In April 1991, the Chili Peppers moved into a historic mansion at 351 Laurel Canyon, Boulevard that was built in 1918."

podcast.body: The Red Hot Chili Peppers signed a new record deal with Warner Brothers, moving from EMI, which coincided with their recording of "Blood Sugar Sex Magik." "They had a new record deal, moving from EMI to Warner Brothers."

podcast.title: Tour Openers for "Blood Sugar Sex Magik" Tour (1991-1992)
podcast.body: During the tour supporting "Blood Sugar Sex Magik," the Red Hot Chili Peppers were joined by two emerging bands as their openers: The Smashing Pumpkins and Pearl Jam, indicating the significant cultural impact and growing status of the Chili Peppers. "One was called The Smash and Pumpkins, and the other was Pearl Jam."

podcast.title: Frusciante's First Departure and Tour Cancellation (May 1992)
podcast.body: The deteriorating internal dynamics within the Red Hot Chili Peppers, exacerbated by John Frusciante's aversion to fame and drug use, culminated in his refusal to perform at Sonic City in Japan on May 7, 1992, declaring he quit. This departure, which the band attributed to Frusciante's mental stress, forced the cancellation of remaining tour dates, including major festival appearances, as an attempt to bring in replacement guitarist Arik Marshall for rehearsals failed due to lack of time. "So the remaining shows in the tour, including a bunch of big festival dates, were canceled."

podcast.title: Lollapalooza 1992 Main Stage Act
podcast.body: The Red Hot Chili Peppers were among the major bands performing on the main stage of the 1992 Lollapalooza Festival, a lineup described as one of the best in the event's history. "the Red Hot Chili Peppers were there."

podcast.title: Post-Frusciante Guitarists and Internal Struggles (1992-1997)
podcast.body: Following John Frusciante's initial departure, the Red Hot Chili Peppers briefly brought in Arik Marshall, who performed with them at Lollapalooza 1992. After Marshall, Jane's Addiction guitarist Dave Navarro was brought in for one album, but his tenure ended unhappily, and he was fired in April 1997. During this period, Anthony Kiedis continued to struggle with sobriety, and Flea was undergoing a messy divorce, adding to the band's stresses. "Dave Navarro was brought in for one album. That's a whole other story that had an unhappy ending."

podcast.title: Wayne's World Soundtrack Contribution (1992)
podcast.body: The Red Hot Chili Peppers were featured on the first *Wayne's World* soundtrack, released in 1992. While the album was primarily composed of classic rock, it notably included tracks from contemporary alternative bands like the Chili Peppers and Soundgarden. "However, it does feature the chili peppers and soundcard."

podcast.title: Dave Navarro's Recruitment (September 1993)
podcast.body: Dave Navarro joined the Red Hot Chili Peppers in September 1993, replacing Jesse Tobias, who had been with the band for less than a year. Navarro had been courted by several bands after Jane's Addiction disbanded, including an offer from Guns N' Roses to replace Izzy Stradlin, which he declined. Although he initially doubted his suitability for the band's funky style, he was persuaded to join. "Dave joined the Chili Peppers in September 1993 as a replacement for Jesse Tobias, who had been with the band for less than a year."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Anthony Kiedis's Rehab and Relapses (1994-1997)
podcast.body: Kiedis's first serious rehab stint led to five years of sobriety, but he relapsed in January 1994 after a wisdom tooth extraction led to prescription narcotics (Vicodin and Percodan) and a return to cocaine and heroin. This cycle of getting straight and relapsing continued until 1997, including a stay at Exodus Recovery Center in Marina Del Rey, California. "His first serious trip to rehab left him sober for five years, but then there was a relapse in January 1994 when he had a wisdom tooth removed and the dentist put him on narcotics for the pain, which was a really bad idea."

podcast.title: Loss of Guitars in House Fire (1996)
podcast.body: In 1996, John Frusciante lost a significant portion of his guitar collection when his house was destroyed by fire. "John had a lot more guitars, but he lost all of them when his house burned down in 1996."

podcast.title: Anthony Kiedis's "Last Chance" Rehab (1997)
podcast.body: A trip to India sparked a spiritual awakening for Anthony Kiedis. Upon returning to Los Angeles in 1997, he checked into a "last chance" rehab place called the Impact Drug and Alcohol Treatment Center in Pasadena for about a month, a facility known for hosting members of Mötley Crüe and Brent Gerowicz of Bad Religion. This visit initially seemed successful. "A trip to India put him in a spiritual place, and when he got back to LA, he checked into a last chance rehab place called the Impact Drug and Alcohol Treatment Center in Pasadena for about a month."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Anthony Kiedis's Motorcycle Accident and Painkiller Addiction (1997)
podcast.body: Following a severe motorcycle accident, Anthony Kiedis was prescribed Codeine, Percocet, and OxyContin. Due to his developed tolerance to chemicals, these medications were ineffective against the pain of nine months of physical rehabilitation for a shattered arm. On his 35th birthday, November 1, 1997, he checked into a rehab unit called Steps, but this attempt was also unsuccessful. "The pain of nine months of physical rehab for a shattered arm were extremely painful."

podcast.title: Band's State in Late 1998
podcast.body: When John Frusciante rejoined in late 1998, the band was in a difficult place, with Flea having issues, Anthony Kiedis battling addictions again, and creative blocks amid divorces and new babies. "The band was not in a good place. Fle was having issues. Anthony was battling addictions again. There were divorces and new babies and creative blocks."

podcast.title: Dave Navarro's Dismissal (Spring 1998)
podcast.body: Dave Navarro was fired in the spring of 1998 due to escalating personal and drug-related conflicts, particularly with Anthony Kiedis, who was attempting to get clean while Navarro was heavily using heroin. Navarro frequently arrived late and high for rehearsals, leading to an argumentative meeting where he fell backwards over an amplifier and stormed out. Bassist Flea's health and relationship issues also contributed to the decision to bring back John Frusciante, ultimately leading to Navarro's ousting. "Dave was out."

podcast.title: John Frusciante's Return (1998)
podcast.body: John Frusciante, who had previously left the band in 1992 and was battling severe heroin addiction, was invited back in 1998. This decision, initiated by Flea, underscored the critical state of the band and the difficulties with Dave Navarro. "The only way the bend can continue is if we get John back. He was talking about John Fruciante, the guy who bailed on them back in 1992 and who was well down the road to killing himself with heroin."

podcast.title: Reunion with John Frusciante (1998)
podcast.body: After Dave Navarro's firing in April 1997, Anthony Kiedis and Flea initiated contact with a recovering John Frusciante. Kiedis visited Frusciante's art gallery, and Flea personally invited him to rejoin the band, expressing great happiness at the prospect. Kiedis even purchased a '62 Stratocaster for Frusciante, who didn't own a guitar at the time. The reunited classic lineup began jamming, writing, and recording demos in Flea's garage in September 1998, signifying Frusciante's return after a six-year absence. "Anthony was the first to reach out by going to a gallery event where John was displaying some of his paintings."

podcast.body: All albums released by the Red Hot Chili Peppers since 1999 are singled out as "big offenders" in the "loudness wars." This means their music, particularly Flea's bass, exhibits noticeable distortion and clipping due to excessive compression during mastering, aimed at making the music sound louder. "anything the Red Hot Chili Peppers have released since 1999."

podcast.title: Performing During Woodstock 99 Fires (1999)
podcast.body: The Red Hot Chili Peppers took the stage at Woodstock 99 on Sunday night amidst a growing mob mentality and escalating violence. A peace group had distributed 100,000 candles for a vigil during their set, but the unruly crowd used these candles to set fires, looting vendor booths, burning plywood walls, and even toppling a speaker tower. The situation was further exacerbated when the band launched into their cover of Jimi Hendrix's "Fire," which seemingly encouraged more arson. "it was probably a really bad idea for the chili peppers to launch into their cover of Jimmy Hendrix's fire, which of course only encouraged more fire."

podcast.body: The Red Hot Chili Peppers embarked on a road trip with Stone Temple Pilots during the "Below Empty" tour in 2000, which covered numerous festivals and generally proceeded smoothly. "The rest of the year was filled with the below empty tour, covering dozens of festivals, a road trip with the Red Hot Chili Peppers, and another with God's Mac, and it all went pretty well."

podcast.body: The Red Hot Chili Peppers performed live in Hyde Park, London, in the summer of 2004, attracting a record-setting 245,000 people over three nights. The series of gigs grossed an impressive $17 million, setting a significant attendance and revenue record for a rock concert. "apparently 245,000 people took in those gigs over three nights."

podcast.title: Band Hiatus and Confidence Crisis (2007-2019)
podcast.body: After the "Stadium Arcadium" tour ended in August 2007, the band agreed to a long rest, with Anthony Kiedis being particularly tired. During John Frusciante's second absence, the band experienced a "crisis of confidence" and felt "lost" in terms of direction and inspiration. "After the long stadium Arcadium tour wrapped up in August 2007, the band agreed to take a nice long rest. Anthony was especially tired and needed the break."

podcast.title: Lower Earnings Despite Extensive Touring (2016)
podcast.body: The Red Hot Chili Peppers, ranked at position 32, undertook an intense tour of over 100 concerts but did not generate as much income as might be expected. This was attributed to significant concert expenses and their participation in numerous charity concerts and donations, which made many of their performances less economically profitable for the band. "han tenido una intensísima gira de más de 100 conciertos, pero no han ingresado tanto."

podcast.title: Classic Lineup Returns (2019-Present)
podcast.body: With John Frusciante back for his third stint, the "classic Red Hot Chili Peppers lineup" is reunited, described as cleaner, more sober, older, and wiser than ever before. "The classic Red Hot Chili Peppers lineup is back together. Everyone is cleaner and more sober than they've ever been. Everyone may be a lot older too but there's certainly a lot wiser."

podcast.body: Flea initiated John Frusciante's third return after secret jamming sessions, and when he brought it up with Anthony and Chad, Josh Klinghoffer was fired within half a second to reinstate Frusciante. podcast.title: COVID-19 Pandemic and Songwriting (2020)
podcast.body: The COVID-19 pandemic provided an unexpected opportunity for the band, with nothing to do but write songs. They wrote constantly from January to October 2020, resulting in over a hundred songs for their new album. "Writing a new album started almost immediately...They wrote constantly from January to October 2020 as COVID raged all around them. As Anthony said, with the pandemic, there was nothing to do but write songs."

podcast.title: "Mother's Milk" Nudity Lawsuit
podcast.body: The cover of *Mother's Milk* sparked controversy due to its depiction of Don Lane, a topless woman cradling the band members. Lane claimed the band did not ask for her permission to use her image. Several record store chains, including Walmart, refused to stock or display the record due to perceived female nudity, despite the minimal exposure. Walmart specifically opted for a censored version where band members were enlarged to cover more of Lane. Compounding the issue, limited promotional posters were distributed with Lane's breasts completely exposed, again without her knowledge. Lane subsequently sued the band and was awarded a $50,000 settlement. "She sued the band and won a settlement of $50,000."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Stories Behind Iconic Album Covers Part 1

podcast.title: 2000s Rock Revival
podcast.body: The Red Hot Chili Peppers are cited as one of the major bands that were "back to life" in the early 2000s, playing a part in the resurgence of rock music's dominance with the public.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Addiction Philosophy and Social Circle
podcast.body: John Frusciante's perspective on his addiction was intrinsically linked to his depression, leading him to believe he should be perpetually on drugs because they brought him happiness. He explicitly stated, "I was very sad and I was always happy when I was on drugs. Therefore I should be on drugs all the time. I was never guilty. I was always proud to be an addict." During this period, his social circle included many drug-using companions, notably the actor River Phoenix, who would soon die, and Al Jourgensen. "I was very sad and I was always happy when I was on drugs. Therefore I should be on drugs all the time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Ahead of Their Time
podcast.body: The band's distinctive punk-funk sound was initially considered "too far ahead of its time," but by the summer of 1989, the alternative rock scene had finally caught up and was ready for their innovative style. "And if we're honest, their punk funk sound had originally been too far ahead of its time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Al Jourgensen's "Give It Away" Remix Involvement
podcast.body: John Frusciante was in the studio with Al Jourgensen when Jourgensen was tasked with creating a new mix of the Red Hot Chili Peppers' hit song "Give It Away." This session became legendary for Jourgensen's bizarre method of remixing, which involved bringing a chicken into the studio, making it stoned with pot smoke, and then adjusting the audio mix based on where the chicken defecated on the mixing board. "Two guys that were definitely badly lost for a long, long time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Albums Affected by Loudness Wars
podcast.body: Many recent albums by the Red Hot Chili Peppers are noted for being louder than usual due to high levels of compression, which adversely affects the listening experience by reducing dynamic range. They are also identified as among the "worst offenders" in the Loudness Wars. "The worst offenders that I found are the Arctic monkeys, the chili peppers, the killers, mues, queens of the Stone Age, and of course Metallica."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Anthony Kiedis as a Drug Buddy
podcast.body: Hillel Slovak's struggles with heroin were exacerbated by his becoming drug buddies with Anthony Kiedis, a situation made worse by Kiedis's openness about his struggles while Slovak kept his addiction secret. "It didn't help that he and Anthony Ketus became drug buddies, and it also didn't help that while Anthony was open about his struggles, Hillel kept his secret."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Anthony Kiedis's Childhood Exposure to Drugs
podcast.body: Anthony Kiedis was sent to live with his father, Blocky, in Los Angeles, who was a bit actor with a side drug operation. By age 12, Anthony knew how to roll joints and grow cannabis, and by 14, he had tried heroin. "By the time he was 12, Anthony knew how to roll the joints and how to grow a finger now so it could be used as a coax boon by 14, Anthony had tried heroin."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Anthony Kiedis's Drug-buying Bridge
podcast.body: Kiedis has never revealed the exact location of the bridge in Los Angeles where he used to buy drugs, fearing it might become an unusual fan shrine. Detective work suggests it is likely a bridge in MacArthur Park leading into Wilshire Boulevard. "He's never said where that bridge is because he's afraid that it might become some kind of weird fan shrine."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Anthony Kiedis's Early Introduction to Sex, Drugs, and Rock and Roll (Childhood)
podcast.body: Anthony Kiedis, born in Grand Rapids, Michigan, moved to California at age 12 to live with his father, Blackie Dammit, who was a bit-part actor and drug dealer in Hollywood. Kiedis was exposed to drugs from a young age; at four, his father blew pot smoke in his face. His father's lifestyle involved frequent clubbing on Sunset Strip and bringing various women home. By age 12, Kiedis was accompanying his father to clubs, using quaaludes given by his father, and even propositioning one of his father's girlfriends, Kimberly, with his father's consent, leading to a sexual encounter while his father watched TV. Keith Moon was also an adult friend and role model to Kiedis during this period. "The Chilling Febrero's with Anthony Kedis, who was introduced to the world of sex, drugs and rock and roll fully by the time he was 12."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Anthony Kiedis's Heroin Addiction
podcast.body: Upon the Red Hot Chili Peppers' formation, Anthony Kiedis's drug habit escalated, with heroin becoming his primary addiction, which he smoked, snorted, and injected. He would disappear from recording sessions for days, becoming a full-blown junkie buying drugs from gang members under a bridge in downtown Los Angeles. "Heroine really was his thing, and I'll smoke it, snort it, and ject it whatever it took."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Anthony Kiedis's Initial Reunion Concerns
podcast.body: Anthony Kiedis was initially apprehensive about John Frusciante rejoining the band, worrying that unresolved past resentments could get in the way of their future success. He felt the need to understand if John's return stemmed from a place of love and creation rather than bitterness. "Anthony was initially worried that past resentments would get in the way of their success."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From Broken Record: The Red Hot Chili Peppers Reunite

podcast.title: Anthony Kiedis's Long-term Sobriety and Health Consequences
podcast.body: By the end of the 1990s, Anthony Kiedis had successfully overcome his addictions and has reportedly remained clean since. However, his past intravenous drug use resulted in a case of Hepatitis C. "All that Ivy drug use resulted in a case of hep C, but at least he's still alive."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Anthony Kiedis's Pre-Reunion Sensation
podcast.body: Anthony Kiedis observed that Flea was not "on fire" or feeling his "best self" in the band's previous incarnation, which led Anthony to independently wonder about John Frusciante's potential involvement again, initially thinking of him writing or producing rather than fully rejoining. This sensation grew despite no communication with John for some time. "I just got the sensation like, it would be really nice if John would get involved."

podcast.body: The asterisk logo of the Rejochile Peppers (Red Hot Chili Peppers) is cited as one of the most frequently tattooed band logos. "Los de los logos más tatuados son el asterisco de la banda de Rejochile Peppers."

podcast.title: Bassist as Leading Instrumentalist - Flea's Prominence
podcast.body: The Red Hot Chili Peppers are noted as a rare band where the bassist, Flea, is considered the leading instrumentalist. This prominence of the bass line is a key characteristic of their sound, even as other instrumental contributions like John Frusciante's guitar work are also critical. "The Chili Peppers are a rare band whose bassist is the leading instrumentalist."

podcast.body: This group was among those that "got caught in this updraft" created by the grunge explosion, benefiting significantly from the increased public and industry attention on alternative music. podcast.title: Beyond Cult Status
podcast.body: By the late 1980s, the Red Hot Chili Peppers were no longer considered merely a cult band, indicating their growing popularity within the alternative music scene. "The Red Hot Chili Peppers were at a cult band anymore."

podcast.title: Breakthrough Albums
podcast.body: The Red Hot Chili Peppers developed their identity over three albums before achieving a breakthrough with *Mother's Milk* and then a major success with *Blood Sugar Sex Magik*. This demonstrates a historical trend where bands were given time to evolve and find their sound before achieving mainstream success. "They discovered themselves through 3 albums before they could deliver a little breakthrough with Mother's Milk and then the Big Breakthrough with Blood Sugar Sex Magic."

podcast.title: Chad Smith's Audition and Background
podcast.body: Chad Smith, a hard-hitting drummer from Detroit, was influenced by the relaxed rhythms of Motown. He was the last of 30 people to audition for the drummer position in 1989. Despite almost not making it through, a connection "clicked" in Flea's mind when they jammed, and Smith has been a member ever since. "He was the last guy in a line of 30 people to audition for the gig when it became available in 1989."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Chad Smith's Reunion Catalyst
podcast.body: The idea for John Frusciante's return was sparked by Chad Smith, who told John at Flea's wedding that he missed playing with him and suggested they, along with Flea, should jam sometime. This casual comment initiated the chain of events leading to John's rejoining the band. "Chad had said something to me when I saw him at Flea's wedding. And he was like, he misses playing with me and him and Flea should jam sometime."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Classification as Alternative
podcast.body: Red Hot Chili Peppers were among the bands identified in the early 1990s as being uniquely difficult to categorize, resulting in their classification under the broad "alternative" music label. "there were the red hot chili peppers... Alternative came to mean difference. It was a basket in which to put bands that defied description."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Collaborative Songwriting Process
podcast.body: The creative process for new material involved a natural flow of ideas among the members. John Frusciante would bring "gems" (ideas, chord progressions, arrangements, vocal melodies) to practice, which would inspire Flea to bring his own contributions. Anthony Kiedis would then go for long drives in his Chevy to generate his parts and add them to the collective "stew." "It's like every time John would bring a gem into practice, you know, flee would feel like, okay, I'll bring a gem."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Collaborative Songwriting Process
podcast.body: The band views drum, bass, and guitar parts as equally important to vocals or song construction, emphasizing freedom and equality for each member to play their best. Songs often start with a riff or groove from one member, or sometimes a complete arrangement brought in by John Frusciante. "in our band, we just we feel that a drum part or a bass part is or a guitar part, it's equal to the vocal or to the or to the construction of the song."

podcast.title: Critique of Speed-Focused Playing
podcast.body: Frusciante argues that focusing on playing faster and creating new techniques hinders emotional progress in music, failing to transmit feeling to listeners and leaving players at an emotional level similar to where Hendrix was decades ago. "People believe that by playing faster and creating new playing techniques, you can progress forward, but then they realize that emotionally, they don't progress at all."

Peligro briefly joined the Red Hot Chili Peppers as drummer in 1988, stepping in after Jack Irons could no longer handle being a Chili Pepper following the heroin overdose death of guitarist Hillel Slovak. podcast.body: Influenced by his jazz studies, Flea developed his distinctive slap bass style, which produced a new, jumpy, funky sound. He also studied Bootsy Collins, a favorite who played in George Clinton's band and Sly & The Family Stone. "Influenced by his years of jazz study Flea developed a style of slapping his bass, which gave everything a new jumpy funky sound."

podcast.body: His inspirations include Jimi Hendrix, Joe Strummer, Captain Beefheart, Frank Zappa, Robert Johnson, Bernard Sumner of New Order, and significantly, John McGeoch of Siouxsie and the Banshees, admired for his varied soundscapes. "And who does he look for for inspiration? Well, we talked about Hendrix, but also Joe Strummer, Captain B. Fart, Frank Zappa, loose legend Robert Johnson, Bernard Sumner of New Order."

podcast.title: Early 1990s Peak and Guitarist Issues
podcast.body: The band peaked "too soon" in the 1990s and faced "guitarist problems" by the time the Alt Nation movement was in full swing, impacting their album quality. "They had peaked too soon in the 1990s and by the time the whole Alt Nation thing was in full swing, they were back to having guitarist problems."

podcast.title: Early Drug Use and Band Departure
podcast.body: John Frusciante joined the Red Hot Chili Peppers at barely 20 years old and rapidly descended into severe drug use, starting with extensive marijuana use and escalating to heroin. During the tour for the "Blood Sugar Sex Magik" album, he began hearing voices instructing him, "You're not going to make it, you have to leave the band now." This led him to quit the band while they were in Japan, returning to California to use heroin full-time as a means to self-medicate his deepening depression. "He started hearing voices while the Chili's were a tour behind the blood sugar sex magic album."

podcast.title: Early Formation and Friendship
podcast.body: Hillel Slovak met Anthony Kiedis, Flea, and original drummer Jack Irons at Fairfax High School in Los Angeles, and by 1983, they were all playing together, forming the core of the Red Hot Chili Peppers. "He was born in Israel, and eventually ended up going to Fairfax High School in Los Angeles, where he met Anthony Ketus, Flea, and original peppers drummer Jack Irons."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Friendship and Songwriting
podcast.body: Anthony Kiedis and Flea first met at Fairfax High School in Hollywood, California. Their initial interaction involved Flea "giving a nookie" to Kiedis's only friend at the school. Early in their career, before the band's widespread fame, they wrote a song together during a backpacking trip in the high sierra areas, inspired by their fear of bears. A second verse was later added in Kiedis's backyard on Laurel Avenue. "We actually Flea and I wrote a song early on together in our career before we became the illustrious Red Hot."

podcast.title: Early Touring Rider – New Underwear and Socks
podcast.body: Dating back to their early 1980s history, the Red Hot Chili Peppers were among the first bands to request new underwear (specifically button-fly boxers) and new socks in their rider. This practical demand addressed the lack of laundry opportunities during extensive tours, especially in their formative years. "One of the first things they learned to ask for was new underwear."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Embracing Imperfections and "Mistreatment"
podcast.body: He purposefully seeks out "wonky, distorted, and weird" tones, believing that imperfections and "mistreating" his guitar can generate cool new sounds, rejecting the pursuit of perfectly clean tones. "John believes that imperfections and mistakes can actually make a musical work better. Trying to get clean tones from a guitar is a bad idea."

podcast.title: Emergence from Fishbone Influence
podcast.body: The Red Hot Chili Peppers coalesced from a group that admired and was influenced by Fishbone's music and approach. "There was this one particular group that loved fishbone and what they were doing, and they eventually coalesced into something called the Red Hot Chili Peppers."

podcast.title: Enduring Popularity (Post-90s)
podcast.body: The Red Hot Chili Peppers are mentioned as one of the acts from the 1990s that never went away, maintaining strong popularity with fans and thereby contributing to the competitive landscape for emerging artists in the 21st century. "Green Day, Blink-182, Chili Peppers, Pearl Jam, Smashing Pumpkins, Food Fighters, even bands that ceased to exist, Stone Temple Pilots, Nirvana, Beastie Boys, for example, continued to be extremely popular with fans."

podcast.title: Evolution of Playing Style
podcast.body: Over time, Flea abandoned his prominent slap-bass style in favor of a more melodic approach, characterized by fewer notes, more motion, and less frantic playing. This shift was influenced by bassists like Simon Gallup of The Cure and Peter Hook of Joy Division. "The slap-style has been all but abandoned in favor of a more melodic approach."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Exceptional Rhythm Section
podcast.body: The band is known for having one of the great rhythm sections in New Rock, formed by Flea on bass and Chad Smith on drums. This "funky rhythm section that rocks" provides a strong foundation for the band's sound. "The Red Hot Chili Peppers featuring the backbone of Flea on bass and Chad Smith on drums and together they form one of the great rhythm sections in all of New Rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Exclusive Vintage Guitar Use
podcast.body: He almost exclusively uses vintage guitars, rejecting any made after 1970. His favorites include a 1962 Red Fender Jaguar, a 1962 Sunburst Fender Stratocaster, a 1955 Stratocaster, a 1955 Gretsch White Falcon, a Yamaha SG, and a 1950s Martin 010 for acoustic work. "Much of his sound is derived from the fact that he plays almost exclusively vintage guitars. If it was made after 1970, he wants nothing to do with it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Extensive Ink
podcast.body: The members of the Red Hot Chili Peppers are generally recognized as "guys who have plenty of ink all over." "The Chili Peppers, guys who have plenty of ink all over."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Fans of Gang of Four
podcast.body: Coming out of Hollywood, the Red Hot Chili Peppers were noted as big fans of Gang of Four, indicating a lineage of funk-infused punk. "The Red Hot Chili Peppers, big fans of the Gang of Four, came out of Hollywood."

podcast.body: Unfortunately, D.H. Peligro's struggles with drug and alcohol demons led to his firing later in 1988, which then paved the way for Chad Smith to join the group as drummer. podcast.title: Flea – Developed Influential Slap Style, Later Evolved Toward Melodic Approach
podcast.body: Flea came to rock bass from a jazz background and developed a highly influential slap bass style. He later evolved toward a more melodic and emotionally expressive approach. podcast.title: Flea's Choice Over PiL
podcast.body: Michael Balzary, known as Flea, chose to form the Red Hot Chili Peppers with his friend Anthony instead of joining Public Image Limited, despite having been offered the bass player position. "Michael Ballzary became known as Flea, and that band he formed with his friend Anthony was the Red Hot Chili Peppers."

podcast.body: John Frusciante believes his guitar playing should always serve the song, focusing on tone, melody, rhythm, and structure rather than flashy, attention-grabbing techniques, especially prominent in his initial tenure with the band. podcast.body: Chad Smith, a hard-hitting and rock-solid drummer, started playing drums at the age of seven in St. Paul, Minnesota. podcast.title: Starting from Scratch for Reunion Rehearsals
podcast.body: John Frusciante made a key suggestion for the reunion: instead of trying to pick up where they left off, the band should go "all the way back" and learn old blues songs and early Red Hot Chili Peppers songs. This approach helped them build basic rock and roll foundations, which made the subsequent writing and playing together feel more natural. "He was like, let's learn some old blue songs and let's learn some really old red hot chili pepper songs."

podcast.title: Woodstock 99 Performance Amidst Chaos (Sunday)
podcast.body: The Red Hot Chili Peppers took the stage on the final night of Woodstock 99, at a point when the festival had devolved into extreme chaos, with the crowd instigating widespread fires and vandalism. Peace Group PAX had distributed 100,000 candles for a vigil, but the mob instead used them to ignite bonfires, looted fire booths, plywood walls, ATM machines, merchandise areas, and even a speaker tower, leading MTV to liken the scene to a "concentration camp." xref.title: Fandom and Joining Red Hot Chili Peppers (1984-1988)
xref.body: At 15, around 1984 when the Red Hot Chili Peppers released their debut album, John Frusciante became a dedicated fan, attending their shows and hoping to speak with guitarist Hillel Slovak. He learned all of their songs. Following Slovak's death in June 1988, and Jack Irons' subsequent departure, Frusciante, then 17, began attracting attention for his guitar skills. He turned down an offer from Frank Zappa due to Zappa's anti-drug stance, briefly joined L.A. punk band Thelonius Monster, but ultimately joined the Chili Peppers in October 1988, after a jam session with Flea. "Legend says that he was three hours into his membership with him, when the Chili Peppers called and said, okay, you got the gig. This was October 1988."

xref.title: Early Red Hot Chili Peppers Dynamics and Drug Use (1989-1991)
xref.body: Upon joining the Red Hot Chili Peppers, Frusciante initially bonded closely with Anthony Kiedis, but their relationship became problematic as Kiedis sought sobriety while Frusciante, a teenager, embraced a wild lifestyle of drinking and drugs, believing it was part of being a "Chili Pepper." He also felt immense pressure to fill Hillel Slovak's shoes. Despite his desire to get high, Frusciante's unique, melodic, "sinewy, slinky, slippery" style of playing was pivotal in transforming the band's sound, making Anthony more comfortable than he had been with Slovak, and influencing Flea's bass playing to become more melodic. "John was this teenager who wanted to drink and do drugs and have sex 24-7. He thought this was how you were supposed to be a Chili Pepper, wild and wacky, in his words."

xref.title: Formation Origin - Pickup Basketball Game (1989)
xref.body: The band's genesis began in Seattle when Stone Gossard and Jeff Ament formed Love Company and sought a singer by circulating a demo. Jack Irons, a former Red Hot Chili Peppers drummer, received a copy of this demo and passed it to Eddie Vedder, a surfer and night shift worker at a Chevron tank farm in San Diego, after a pickup basketball game in 1989. Eddie then wrote lyrics to three of the demo's five songs, dubbed them onto a new cassette, and sent it to Seattle, leading to his invitation to jam with the group and the formation of Pearl Jam. "This cassette passed out of a gym bag sometime in 1989 might have resulted in the most profitable pickup basketball game ever played."

xref.body: In May 1992, in the middle of a tour of Japan, John Frusciante quit the Red Hot Chili Peppers due to becoming angry and disillusioned with fame. For the next six years, he descended into a severe heroin addiction and abject poverty, which led to a house fire and health issues that nearly killed him. xref.title: First Departure from Red Hot Chili Peppers (May 7, 1992)
xref.body: After escalating tensions, interviews he hated, and feeling reduced to a "performing monkey," John Frusciante refused to go on stage at Sonic City in Japan on May 7, 1992, just minutes before a show was to begin. He declared, "I quit," citing an inability to do justice to his creations and hearing voices telling him to leave. Although he reluctantly played that final, poor-quality 15-song set, it marked his last show with the Chili Peppers for six years. The band explained his departure as an inability to cope with mental stress. "I've reached the stage where I cannot do justice to what I've created. I can't give you what it takes to be in this band anymore."

xref.title: Livid Over Saturday Night Live Performance (1992)
xref.body: Anthony Kiedis was "livid" and believed John Frusciante "sabotaged everything" during the Red Hot Chili Peppers' "Saturday Night Live" performance. He felt betrayed by Frusciante's "dissonant out of tune experiment" during "Under the Bridge," especially given the live television audience. He confronted Frusciante after the show, suspecting heroin use. "I felt like I was getting stabbed in the back and hung up to drive in front of all of America. While this guy was off in a corner in the shadow, playing some dissonant out of tune experiment."

xref.title: Post-Quitting Reflection and Life as a Junkie (1992-1996)
xref.body: After leaving the Red Hot Chili Peppers in 1992, John Frusciante auditioned for the Meat Puppets, but it didn't work out. He subsequently fell into a deep depression, becoming a full-fledged heroin addict. At 23, he felt his life and music career were over, and he didn't pick up a guitar for a period. For three years, he rarely left his Hollywood home, which deteriorated, covered in graffiti. He used heroin heavily, stating he was "proud to be an addict" and happy only when on drugs. He neglected to cash royalty checks, including one for $600,000, found by Flea's daughters. "I was very sad and I was always happy when I was on drugs. Therefore I should be on drugs all the time."

xref.title: Recovery and Rejoining Red Hot Chili Peppers (1996-1998)
xref.body: John Frusciante quit heroin cold turkey in late 1996, after five years of constant use, though he continued using crack for a couple more years. In January 1998, a friend convinced him to seriously enter rehab. He faced a lethal mouth infection requiring all his rotted teeth to be pulled out and replaced with $75,000 worth of implants to prevent sepsis, as well as skin grafts for abscesses on his arms. After rehab worked, Anthony Kiedis reached out to him at a gallery event showcasing his paintings, and Flea personally invited him to rejoin the band. Frusciante, who didn't even own a guitar, was bought a '62 Stratocaster by Kiedis. The band reassembled in Flea's garage in September 1998, where they began jamming, writing, and recording demos, including an early version of "Californication." "John was rusty both physically and mentally. They started jamming and they started writing."

xref.title: 606 Studios: The All-Purpose Hub (Northridge, California)
xref.body: In 2005, following the success of the "One by One" album, the Foo Fighters invested $750,000 to establish their 8,000-square-foot 606 Studios (also known as 606 West) in Northridge, California. Dave Grohl describes it as the "all-purpose Foo Fighters hub" where they rehearse, store gear, record albums, and host press events. The studio, originally a warehouse and once the home of a woman being stalked, was inspired by ABBA's Polar Studios and prominently features the recording console from the legendary Sound City Studios, used by Nirvana, Red Hot Chili Peppers, Rage Against the Machine, Slipknot, and Tom Petty. "By the time the Fuzc got to the one by one album in 2005, they had enough money to invest in their own recording studio in Northridge, California. They call it 606 Studios."

His concern was that any past resentments could potentially impede the band's success. "Anthony was initially worried that past resentments would get in the way of their success."

xref.title: Jack Irons' Collaboration – During Matt Cameron's Soundgarden Tenure
xref.body: Jack Irons, who was once a drummer for Eleven and briefly for the Red Hot Chili Peppers, worked with Pearl Jam at a time when Matt Cameron was performing with Soundgarden. Irons also played a crucial role in Eddie Vedder joining the band by passing along a demo tape. "Jack would later join the Red Hot Chili Peppers for a bit, and he worked with Pearl Jam when Matt Cameron went off with Soundgarden."

xref.title: Jack Irons' Drumming Role – Early Member
xref.body: Jack Irons, who later joined the Red Hot Chili Peppers and worked with Pearl Jam, was a drummer for Eleven at one point. His connections to the Seattle music scene further highlight the interconnectedness of many of the era's bands. "There Elaine and a friend named Natasha Schneider formed a group called Eleven, which at one point had a drummer named Jack Irons."

xref.title: Kurt Cobain's Bond with John Frusciante
xref.body: When Nirvana opened some shows for the Red Hot Chili Peppers, John Frusciante found a "soulmate" in Kurt Cobain. They bonded over a shared desire for their bands to remain "cool and underground," which exacerbated Frusciante's dissatisfaction with the Chili Peppers' mainstream success. "John found a soulmate in Kurt Cobain, a guy who also wanted his band to stay cool in underground."

xref.title: Les Claypool's Bass-Driven Style
xref.body: Primus's music, a mix of alternative metal and funk metal, is primarily built around the distinctive bass grooves of singer and bass player Les Claypool. Claypool is described as an inventive player, unafraid to push boundaries, with a style comparable to Geddy Lee of Rush crossed with Flea of the Red Hot Chili Peppers. "Primus, experiments with a mix of alternative metal and funk metal, all built around singer and bass player Les Claypool's grooves. Great player, very inventive, never afraid to push boundaries."

xref.title: Mellotron Usage
xref.body: O'Brien owned and used a Mellotron, a "taped piano" instrument, famously on the Red Hot Chili Peppers' album "Blood Sugar Sex Magik" and specifically on their song "Breaking the Girl." He later used this same Mellotron on Billy Talent's songs "Saint Veronica" and "White Sparrows" from the album "Billy Talent III," after the band expressed their admiration for its sound.

xref.title: Member of SOS All Stars
xref.body: Roger Taylor joined Taylor Hawkins and Chad Smith in the one-off drummers' group SOS All Stars for the Live Earth show in London in 2007. This performance brought together influential drummers for a special event. "He was joined by Roger Taylor, of course, and Chad Smith of the Red Hot Chili Peppers."

xref.title: Mohican Ancestry
xref.body: Anthony Kiedis of the Red Hot Chili Peppers has stated that there is Mohican heritage somewhere in his family tree. "Anthony Ketus of the Red Hot Chili Peppers says somewhere in his family tree is Mohican heritage."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Multiple Departures and Returns
xref.body: John Frusciante has had a complicated relationship with the Red Hot Chili Peppers, being in and out of the band multiple times over 30 years. He initially joined in October 1988, left in May 1992, rejoined by the end of the 90s (specifically, demos recorded in September 1998), and is noted to have left and returned again, making his tenure with the band "complicated." "Yes, he's back in the Chili Peppers by the end of the 90s, but he would leave again. And he would come back again."

xref.title: Musical Activities During Hiatus
xref.body: During his time away from the Red Hot Chili Peppers, John Frusciante was primarily focused on making electronic music. However, he continued practicing guitar consistently, maintaining his instrumental skills. "Practicing guitar is something I was always doing even though I'm making electronic music."

xref.title: Nudity in "What's My Age Again?" Video
xref.body: The music video for "What's My Age Again?" depicted the band members running around Los Angeles appearing naked, though they were actually wearing flesh-colored speedos. The band later expressed dissatisfaction with this image, aiming to avoid being typecast as a "joke band" or compared to the Red Hot Chili Peppers, and vowed to take more creative control over their public image. "They wanted to leave nudity to the Red Hot Chili Peppers, and they did not want to be viewed as a joke band, so they vowed to take more creative control when it came to their public image."

xref.title: Reunion Rehearsal Strategy
xref.body: John Frusciante proposed a specific strategy for the band's initial reunion rehearsals: learning old blues songs and early Red Hot Chili Peppers songs. This foundational approach aimed to relearn "basic rock and roll kind of building blocks" from scratch, which proved instrumental in making the new writing process feel more natural. "John made some really wise suggestions in the very beginning. He was like, let's learn some old blue songs and let's learn some really old red hot chili pepper songs."

xref.body: Jacob Dylan has been the sole consistent member of The Wallflowers throughout its existence, a band that remains active today. The lineup has seen several changes, with notable past members including Jack Irons, formerly of the Red Hot Chili Peppers and Pearl Jam, and Rami Jaffee, keyboardist for Foo Fighters.
